description: Istanbul Atatürk High School of Science
summary:
CrewPulse is a health app for astronauts on long missions. Every day, the astronaut spends a few minutes taking measurements: heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood, vision and attention. The app compares the results with the person's own normal, warns early if something changes and says what to do.

In space, the body slowly weakens, and the astronaut often does not notice it. When a problem appears, the doctor is very far away. On the way to Mars, an answer can take more than 40 minutes.

CrewPulse also uses real NASA data. Solar storms from NASA DONKI and Fermi GBM, and radiation measurements from the TEPC instrument on the ISS, appear on the same screen as the health data. If there is a storm, the app sends the astronaut to the shelter.

What makes CrewPulse different is that its advice changes with how far the crew is from Earth. For example, when an astronaut's heart rate is much higher than their own normal, the app on the ISS says "measure again and send the result to the flight surgeon", because the doctor can answer within seconds. During Mars transit, the same result leads to "follow the steps in the app, tell the crew medical officer first, then report to Earth", because an answer from Earth can take more than 40 minutes.

CrewPulse does not diagnose. It gives early warning and guidance, so the astronaut knows what to do even when the doctor is far away.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

CrewPulse works in four steps: measure, understand, connect and decide.

1. Measure. Every day, the astronaut spends a few minutes entering 22 measurements, including heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, sleep, mood, vision and attention. The measurements are asked one at a time. Next to each one, the app shows the normal range, a picture that explains how to measure it and why it matters. Astronauts are not expected to be medical experts, so we explained every step clearly.

2. Understand. Everyone's normal is different. For someone whose heart rate is usually 60, 85 is high, but in general tables 85 looks normal. That is why the app compares every new measurement with the astronaut's last 20 measurements. If a value is far from the person's own normal, the app catches it and says which value it is. It then gives a health score from 0 to 100. If there is even one serious problem, the score cannot go above 49. The status is shown with colour, text and pattern together, so someone who cannot tell colours apart can still understand it.

3. Connect. Each time the server starts, it downloads solar storm records for the last 30 days from NASA DONKI and solar flares from the Fermi GBM list. Daily radiation on the ISS is 0.884 mSv, based on measurements from the TEPC instrument. These events appear on the same chart as the health data, so if sleep or attention got worse during a solar storm, it is easy to see. If a storm starts, the app raises the alert level and sends the astronaut to the shelter. On the ISS, the shelter reduces storm radiation by about 96% compared with the least protected part of the station.

4. Decide. This step is the heart of our project. The app first looks at how serious the situation is: normal day, measure again, act now or emergency. Then it looks at where the crew is. There are 5 mission settings: the ISS, a lunar transit spacecraft, a lunar surface base, a pressurized lunar rover and Mars transit. On the ISS the ground team decides, on the Moon the crew and the ground team decide together, and during Mars transit the crew acts first on its own. For example, our demo astronaut Mira Sato's heart rate is usually 75. When it reads 101 one morning, the app says her heart rate is 34% above her own normal. On the ISS, the advice is "measure again within 2 hours and send the result to the flight surgeon". During Mars transit, it says "measure again now, tell the crew medical officer, do not wait for Earth".

Other features:

- Body map: divides the body into 12 regions and shows the status of each region with colour. Clicking a region opens its measurements.

- Gravity risk analysis: scores 12 risks of weightlessness by likelihood and impact, and shows upcoming checks in a calendar.

- Bone loss forecast: based on monthly rates from scientific studies. 120 minutes of exercise a day reduces this loss by up to half.

- Activity plan: changes every day based on sleep, mood and the latest measurements.

- Mind Lab: a short survey, a 3-minute attention test and eight short games. It is inspired by the Cognition test battery developed for NASA at the University of Pennsylvania.

- Trends: charts that show how the measurements change over the days.

What are the benefits?

The astronaut notices a change in their health before it turns into a problem. Even when they cannot reach a doctor right away, they know the next step. The ground team receives a short, clear summary instead of long lists of numbers. The app does not only warn when a problem appears; it also helps the astronaut stay strong with a daily exercise plan.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is for an astronaut far from Earth to be able to track their own health and make the right decision. This will be very important on long missions such as Mars. The same idea can also be used in places on Earth that are far from doctors, such as research stations in Antarctica, ships and rural areas.

What tools did we use?

- Server: written in Rust.

- Database: SQLite. All rules and texts are stored in the database, so they can be updated without changing the code.

- Data tools: Python, used to download NASA data and prepare the database.

- Personal normal model: built with TensorFlow. The live version uses a lighter statistical method (z-score).

- Interface: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It works in English and Turkish and has a night view.

- Deployment: the app runs publicly on Render with Docker.

- Tests: 10 JavaScript, 16 Python and 12 Rust tests pass.

- Licence: the project is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence.

How is our project creative?

Most health apps compare people with general averages and give the same advice everywhere. CrewPulse does three things differently:

1. It compares the astronaut with their own normal.

2. It changes its advice based on how far the crew is from Earth.

3. It shows NASA space weather data in the same place as the health data.

We also turned the daily check-in into a habit with badges, a days-in-a-row count and game-like tests.

What factors did we consider?

- Safety: CrewPulse does not diagnose. It is an early warning and guidance tool and does not replace the crew medical officer or a doctor.

- Scientific basis: health limits, bone loss rates and cabin air levels are based on 57 scientific sources, most of them from the NASA Human Research Program and NASA-STD-3001.

- Ease of use: the daily check-in is short, the language is simple and every measurement is explained with a picture.

- Accessibility: the status is shown with colour, text and pattern. There is a night mode and two languages.

- Data honesty: the solar storm and radiation data are real NASA data. The demo astronaut Mira Sato and her measurements are sample data, because the health data of real astronauts is confidential.

- Privacy: the NASA key is not in the code; it is stored in the server settings. The app never sends any information anywhere automatically.

Live app: https://iafl-crewpulse.onrender.com (the first load may take about a minute)
